approach.method_basis: The Parent first trains a recurrent SMILES prior on unlabeled molecules. Each objective starts a fresh adaptable copy and alternates one neural proposal batch with two graph-breeding batches. Accepted neural molecules refresh a scored breeding population, with a real fresh neural parent protected at the first graph handoff. A fingerprint Gaussian posterior trained only on that objective's accepted scores samples functions over fresh offspring pools to choose the remaining graph evaluations. Accepted graph trajectories then train the neural policy through trajectory balance, a learned normalizer and regularization toward the unchanged prior. The reusable prior still learns only the supplied molecular strings, even though the online neural sampler must compose new strings.
approach.novelty: Expose the unlabeled prior to two identity-equivalent traversals of a molecule: retain its original string and sometimes train on one checked atom-order alternative. This broadens the local sequence contexts in which the same molecular structure is learned without changing the molecule allocation or adding scored data. Neither sibling has changed prior serialization support; their difference was graph-offspring selection. The online learning, graph edits and posterior selector remain exactly as in the current Parent, so this experiment asks whether a less serialization-specific starting distribution supplies better material to the existing reciprocal search.

nodes.hypothesis: Train the reusable unlabeled recurrent prior on a half-original, half identity-checked alternative-SMILES serialization mixture for the same selected training rows, preserving the original holdout checkpoint rule and all online components.

finding_summary.headline: Alternative-traversal support and scores improve, while raw neural validity worsens
finding_summary.insights: This establishes broader support for equivalent molecular traversals, with a measurable cost in fitting the original strings. That support does not automatically make adapted neural generation more chemically valid or improve every task. The higher overall score coexists with more invalid draws and with chemically questionable high-scoring structures: the Molecular assessment identifies an unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur family in the largest-gain task, selenium-containing aromatic amines elsewhere, poor size control and absent stereochemical specification. The gain therefore cannot be interpreted as a general chemical-quality improvement, nor as evidence that selenium or the atypical sulfur connectivity is necessary. The experiment isolates the changed preparation mechanism in source, but its downstream effects pass through the inherited reciprocal graph search and posterior selection; the logged first neural batches already follow initial-observation adaptation and are not a pure-prior test. The useful new distinction is between learning more traversal syntax, sampling valid molecules, and obtaining favorable scalar scores. All three must remain visible.
finding_summary.results: The intended preparation mechanism activated in every seed. About 3.786 million changed-alternative exposures entered gradient minibatches per completed preparation, and more than 99.5% of the distinct consumed alternative rows added adjacent-token contexts absent from their own original strings. The original molecular row schedule and holdout split were preserved, with identity and encoding checks backed by independently reconstructed logged pairs and the full holdout. Learned support broadened: on the same held-out alternative traversals, token NLL falls from the Parent’s 1.76–1.78 to about 0.765, and the alternative-versus-original gap shrinks from about 1.19–1.22 to 0.157–0.159. Original-string fit worsens, from about 0.563–0.566 to 0.607, despite both nodes completing the same 29,742 training steps. Preparation takes about 1,056–1,071 seconds versus 218–281 seconds for the Parent. All online code and prior-freezing checks remain intact. All required evaluations finish, and all three seed macro scores improve: the mean rises from 0.520669 to 0.546307, a paired gain of 0.025638, with individual gains of 0.010517, 0.025244 and 0.041153. The benefit is uneven across tasks: the sitagliptin mean rises by 0.163551, while three other task means decline. Raw neural validity also falls from 70.34% to 61.88%; invalid and unterminated strings rise even though every announced batch is filled.

The two artifact files were independently hashed and the complete content digest checked against formal seed-N/candidate_execution.json. Each prior.pt was loaded with weights_only=True on CPU and every tensor hash recomputed. The independent likelihood audit used only forward passes of these existing selected checkpoints on exactly the original/alternative heldout pairs; it made no oracle calls, optimizer updates, new sampling runs or checkpoint choices. Token denominators and total sequence NLL are preserved separately for original and alternative strings. CPU FP32 and original CUDA mixed-precision values are labeled separately. Full preparation evidence, all 61 validation points for each of the six preparations, selected-checkpoint counters, diagnostics, pair/row-schedule hashes and read-only paired likelihoods are in .slots/SPIRAL2.r0008-03-improve-L07.analysis-prior-audit.json. Preparation source and log points establish that only unweighted original holdout loss selected the state, and that all three runs reached 29,742 steps within the unchanged deadline. The seed-0 preparation reused from smoke is identified by its formal prepared-artifact hash; its smoke score is never used as research evidence. Every Parent and Child seed-N/logs/TASK.log was scanned for initialization, flow_replay_complete, genetic_flow_feedback, genetic_flow_observation, policy_trajectory_generated and genetic_flow_batch evidence. These join to all 9,000 accepted trajectory records across the two nodes with exact canonical identities and observed scores. All 30 objective initializations and 900 replay-complete receipts preserve the respective prior. Per-seed and first-versus-later neural counters, event line references, task scores and trusted paired aggregation are in .slots/SPIRAL2.r0008-03-improve-L07.analysis-log-audit.json. Score values come from the completed summary.json files and scripts.policy_core.evidence._aggregate/_paired_delta against the Parent ledger. The context.molecular_assessment supplies chemical interpretation, including unusual sulfur/selenium families and missing configurations; it is not substituted for the mechanism or score audit. No candidate source, prepared checkpoint, data, evaluator or completed replica was edited or rerun during analysis.

molecular.headline: Rich aromatic and nitrogen-ring chemistry, with new selenium and unusual sulfur families, uneven size control and unspecified stereochemistry.
molecular.overall_character: The supplied trajectories contain 4,500 evaluated molecules, including 4,350 optimizer proposals, across all three supplied replicas and all five tasks; the same 4,500 parent rows were read for comparison. The repertoire includes fused nitrogen heterocycles, phenols, carbonyl-containing rings, diarylamines, saturated amine rings, aryl alkynes and selenium heteroaromatics. All 4,350 emitted child SMILES parsed with the supplied RDKit environment, but graph validity is distinct from synthetic plausibility. The digest ring-closure rates range from 0.9839 to 0.9908 and aromatic-marker rates from 0.9609 to 0.9793; these are string-level presence counters, not aromatic atom fractions. Read-only RDKit measurements on optimizer rows give median heavy-atom counts of 26, 43, 29, 34 and 26 in the brief task order. Useful-looking medium-sized medicinal chemistry coexists with very small fragments, oversized linked assemblies, unusual heteroatom connectivity and strained-looking ring edits. Several seed-specific leading families differ substantially from the Parent, while many leading neighbors within each family remain close relatives. The structural-diversity judgment is therefore moderate despite numerous distinct molecular graphs. Every task has stereocentre_rate 0.0; RDKit detects unassigned tetrahedral centres in 290, 215, 433, 511 and 298 optimizer rows respectively, and assigned tetrahedral centres in none. The observations describe output chemistry; they do not establish the cause of its change, a synthetic route, or measured stability.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest digest examples are medium-sized fused aryl/nitrogen systems: a phenyl-substituted indazole-like N-carbamoyl core fused to a gem-dimethyl oxygen ring, followed by phenolic diaryl pyrazoline-like compounds. The leading structure has 24 heavy atoms and four perceived rings, three aromatic. Seed 0 also explores aryl ureas and sulfur-linked carbamoyl groups attached to a four-membered unsaturated nitrogen ring bearing an aldehyde. Across optimizer rows the median is 26 heavy atoms and three rings, with 624 distinct nonchiral Murcko scaffolds; the Parent had medians of 25 heavy atoms and three rings and 529 such scaffolds. These counts include small ring edits and do not demonstrate an equivalent number of synthetically useful core families. The Parent high tail instead included biaryl pyrazole/acetanilide and quinoline/urea arrangements. Thus the new output changes the core families while retaining extensive aromatic, donor/acceptor and carbonyl chemistry.
liabilities: Aldehyde-bearing four-membered unsaturated nitrogen rings and sulfur-linked variants need chemical scrutiny; their accepted graphs and scores do not establish accessible or stable compounds.

Both tiny heteroatom fragments and much larger flexible assemblies consume part of the observed proposal set. Sixty-five of the 870 optimizer rows contain a bond from N, O or S directly to a halogen, compared with 34 Parent rows under the same bond-based count.
Repeated phenol, heteroatom and ring-closure edits can change reactivity or geometry even when much of the favorable aromatic framework remains.
missing_features: Reliable exploration of compact alternative cores that preserves the useful aryl, nitrogen and carbonyl arrangement remains incomplete; many surrounding edits lose the favorable combination rather than cleanly substitute another core.
The pyrazoline-like saturated centres and other substituted ring junctions lack explicit stereochemical specification. No preferred configuration can be inferred from these observations.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The fused N-carbamoyl leader scores 0.4811252243246881, its extra-phenol analogue 0.4588069837338257, and its ring-oxygen-deleted relative 0.458386638264238. Replacing the N-carbamoyl group by methyl in a late relative gives 0.387244764147529; extending one geminal methyl substituent to ethyl gives 0.34636729936804345. These local observations favor a particular compact ring/substituent arrangement, not indiscriminate heteroatom addition. A phenolic pyrazoline-like molecule scores 0.4201182934804424, while the aldehyde/aryl-urea family reaches 0.40910891241125485. In contrast, Cl, OO and OF each score 0.0, and a very large flexible polyamine/polyaryl molecule scores 1.8344487388079707e-40. The pooled median is 0.129972. Whole-molecule size and functional-group placement both matter in the observed gradient; these data do not identify a uniquely missing target scaffold.

per_task.generated_character: The digest high tail is concentrated in compact, mostly planar triazole-substituted aminopyridine pairs decorated with fluorine and chlorine. The leader has 23 heavy atoms and three aromatic rings, with a diarylamine bridge and several ring nitrogens. Its close relatives change small alkyl groups, halogen positions or fusion to the triazole. These look more conventional as synthetic targets than many of the large late seed-2 carbonyl/thione/sulfur-rich fused assemblies, although no routes are supplied. The full proposal distribution is much larger than its leading family: the child median is 43 heavy atoms and five rings, versus 36 and four in the Parent; 347 of 870 child proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms, versus 128 in the Parent. The digest mean SMILES length is 85.5, maximum 197, and charged-marker rate 0.1724. Parent leading families included heteroaryl amino and acylhydrazone/imine connections; the new compact triazole/aminopyridine family changes their linkage chemistry without eliminating the large-assembly tail.
liabilities: The larger population contains extensive polyaromatic fusion, sulfur/carbonyl linkages, conjugated exocyclic unsaturation and multiple charges or ionizable groups. Their combined synthesis and physical-property balance are unestablished.
Halogen-rich heteroaromatic leaders are plausible motifs, but their observed scores do not demonstrate favorable solubility, stability or the utility of additional halogenation.
New short ring closures and fused arrangements can change geometry sharply. Unassigned tetrahedral centres occur in 215 of the 870 child proposals, with no assigned centres.
missing_features: Compact alternatives that change the core or bridge while retaining the useful heteroaromatic arrangement are not well represented among the leading examples; most quoted leaders decorate the same aminopyridine/triazole family.

Controlled variation between compact and elaborated structures is uneven. The many large assemblies do not establish a missing objective-specific group, and their size is not required by the compact leading examples.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The methyl-, ethyl- and differently halogenated triazole/aminopyridine examples all score 0.6220806794055203. A less halogenated close relative scores 0.6203208556149733, and an additional heteroaromatic ring gives 0.6203675187352428. The narrow spread suggests that local decoration changes do little once that ring/linker arrangement is present. A much larger late carbonyl-rich fused heterocycle still scores 0.6048855296308467, so large size is not uniformly rejected. Nevertheless, the bulky sulfone/amide/cyclic-amine low example scores 0.2889922015596881, and a very heavily brominated polyaromatic assembly scores 0.29217856536262243. The pooled median is 0.574287. These comparisons support useful heteroaromatic connectivity rather than a simple rule to maximize rings, halogens or size.

per_task.generated_character: The pooled high tail is an arylpiperazine/alkylamine family attached to chlorinated benzoselenophene-like rings. Many examples combine an aryl- or pyridyl-substituted piperazine with an additional tertiary amine and a flexible carbon linker. The leading example has 31 heavy atoms and four rings; a simpler high-scoring relative has 25 heavy atoms, a propyl linker and one arylpiperazine. Read-only atom counts find selenium in 174 of 870 child proposals, versus none of the 870 Parent proposals for this task. Other child seeds reach oxygen/carbonyl aromatic systems linked to saturated amines and sulfur/nitrogen heteroaromatics with substituted piperidines. The broader class of accessible saturated amines plus aromatic surfaces was already present in the Parent, whose leaders included diaryl aminoalkyl piperidines and linked saturated amine rings. The child median is 29 heavy atoms and four rings; the aromatic-marker rate is 0.9609. Its low charged-marker rate, 0.0149, does not mean basic centres are absent, because the molecules are written as neutral amines.
liabilities: The selenium heterocycle is unusual within the supplied Parent repertoire and adds an element-specific chemical liability that has not been assessed for stability or synthesis. It should not be called infeasible solely because it contains selenium.
Multiple basic centres, long flexible linkers and repeated aromatic units may complicate physical-property balance. The score alone does not establish those properties.
Some relatives add strained-looking short closures across aromatic frameworks, N–N connections or N–Cl bonds. The leading branched structures also leave tetrahedral configuration unspecified.
missing_features: No further required functional group can be inferred from a high tail already close to the score limit. Saturated basic centres, heteroaromatics and aromatic surfaces are represented.

Defined configurations and systematic linker geometry are not demonstrated for the branched amine family. The present data show missing stereochemical representation, without identifying a rewarded configuration.

Chemically matched conventional alternatives to the selenium-containing family are not established as a controlled comparison. Their absence prevents attributing the favorable whole-molecule score to the unusual element.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The extended pyridylpiperazine/tertiary-amine/selenium structure scores 0.9999994775753148, while the simpler propyl-linked arylpiperazine scores 0.9999993561334308. Removing the extra tertiary-amine branch still permits 0.9999980741980992 in a close family. Conversely, duplication into a much larger polyamine/selenium assembly gives only 0.03431111746034991, and the N-chlorinated nitrogen-ring example scores 0.00036530897832142426. The nitrofuran ester low example scores 6.212341904497256e-05 and an amide-rich heterocycle scores 7.81343751377966e-05. The visible association is with the whole aryl/saturated-amine/linker arrangement, rather than nitrogen count or maximal elaboration. Parent molecules without selenium already reach 0.9999986918258995, so the trajectory does not establish a selenium requirement or a chemically meaningful benefit from tiny differences near the upper score limit.

per_task.generated_character: The leading seed-2 family combines an ethoxy-substituted fused conjugated carbonyl core with N-methylpiperazine, fluorine and an aryl or five-membered N–N/carbonyl appendage. Ring perception identifies a seven-membered conjugated carbonyl ring fused to a six-membered ring in the two strongest cited examples. The leader has 37 heavy atoms and five rings, including an N-phenyl-substituted saturated N–N/carbonyl ring; a near-equal example has 34 heavy atoms, a bromophenyl group and a propionyl substituent instead. Other seeds explore densely fused carbonyl heterocycles and sulfonylated saturated nitrogen rings. These retain the Parent broad pattern of aromatic, carbonyl and saturated nitrogen-ring chemistry, but with different fused cores. The child median is 34 heavy atoms and five rings, compared with 36 and five for the Parent. The digest mean SMILES length is 63.8 and maximum 152. Common medicinal-chemistry substituents are present, while the complete leading frameworks remain elaborate and configurationally unresolved.
liabilities: Large fused conjugated carbonyl systems, multiple appended rings and rearranged short closures can make synthesis and geometry difficult to interpret; no route or conformational assessment is present.

The late high-scoring oxygen-fluorine analogue scores 0.21440741901011376 despite its unusual O–F bond. A favorable observation is therefore compatible with chemically concerning functional-group connectivity.
Duplication of substantial core fragments increases bulk without preserving the leading score in the cited late example. Several important saturated positions remain stereochemically unspecified.
missing_features: Less encumbered alternative cores that retain the favorable carbonyl/aryl/amine relationships have not been explored consistently in the leading neighborhood; near-equal simpler appendage choices show that additional ring complexity is not automatically helpful.

Configurationally specified variants of the substituted saturated N–N/carbonyl rings are missing. RDKit identifies two unassigned tetrahedral centres in the leading molecule and at least one unassigned centre in 511 of 870 child proposals.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The N-phenyl N–N/carbonyl appendage scores 0.22243686751733371 and the bromophenyl/propionyl alternative scores 0.22234616366476415. A benzyl-substituted N–N/carbonyl analogue scores 0.22082458431832067; the simpler bromophenyl/methyl relative scores 0.22050990442479085. These small differences do not establish that the extra saturated nitrogen ring or maximum carbonyl count is essential. The supplied Parent leading values include 0.2124137877466535 for a different fused carbonyl/amine architecture. A heavily duplicated late aromatic/carbonyl assembly scores 0.15308748742436262, while a one-carbon-linked close analogue retains 0.21606790785072147. Methane, OF and difluoromethanol each score 0.0, and a small acyclic fluorinated carbonate-containing molecule scores 0.018771276394456953. The observed preference is for connected aromatic, carbonyl and nitrogen environments; the data do not reveal a specific absent target fragment.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest seed-1 family consists of fluorinated pyridyl–aryl alkynes bearing an oxygen-linked fluoromethyl group and an unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur centre. In the leading SMILES that sulfur has an oxo bond, two nitrogen bonds, one carbon substituent and an explicit hydrogen; this is not the ordinary tetrahedral sulfonamide connectivity one might assume from a casual reading. The leader has 25 heavy atoms and two aromatic rings. The [SH] text occurs in 160 of 870 child optimizer proposals, versus one Parent proposal for this task. Seed 2 instead reaches an N-methylated dicarbonyl nitrogen heterocycle linked through a fluorinated enone to a large conjugated nitrogen-containing ring; other output includes fused lactam/thiol chemistry. The Parent leading families included N-acyl triazolyl azetidines and hydrazino or nitroso-bearing nitrogen compounds. The output therefore changes its nitrogen/fluorine chemistry substantially, but the newer high sulfur family still lacks demonstrated ordinary chemical plausibility. Across optimizer rows the median is 26 heavy atoms and three rings, versus 24 and three in the Parent.
liabilities: Hydrogen-bearing, highly coordinated sulfur environments and variants with additional N–S/O–N connections need explicit chemical review before being treated as practical molecules. RDKit parsing does not establish their stability or preparation.

Seventy-two of the 870 emitted structures have a direct N/O/S–halogen bond under a bond-based count, compared with 26 Parent structures. The cited O–F-containing high example shows that such connectivity is not confined to the low tail.

The alternative high family includes conjugated enones and large conjugated nitrogen rings; variants acquire N–F or additional ring fusion. These are possible reactivity and geometry concerns, with no supplied experimental assessment.
missing_features: Stable, ordinary-valence alternatives that preserve the useful local aryl/alkyne/nitrogen/fluorine arrangement are not established for the leading sulfur family. It would be incorrect to diagnose a general absence of nitrogen, fluorine or carbonyl chemistry.
Core changes that preserve that compact functional-group arrangement remain inconsistent; some late multiplication or relocation of otherwise familiar motifs leads to extremely low scores.

Stereochemically specified saturated and bridged alternatives are absent elsewhere in the output. These observations do not identify an objective-preferred configuration or prove that one particular missing heterocycle is required.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The fluorinated aryl-alkyne structure with the unusual sulfur centre scores 0.5600222476080907. Its otherwise corresponding phenyl analogue without that aryl fluorine scores 0.5113964873062803, and shortening the sulfur-bound fluoroethyl group to fluoromethyl gives 0.4963704929462404 in the aryl-fluorinated family. A longer diyne relative scores 0.5252583563261087. Replacing the oxygen-linked fluoromethyl group by a direct O–F substituent still gives 0.4963704929462404, illustrating that this gradient does not certify normal reactivity. The separate dicarbonyl/enone family reaches 0.4853564671811107. In contrast, a large fluorinated polyaryl/alkyne assembly scores 0.0, a long polar guanidine/amide assembly scores 3.920867438776822e-82, and duplication of the late enone/heterocycle framework gives 2.250908533370224e-18. The pooled median is only 0.001751. Size, polar-group placement and exact connectivity are sharply consequential in these observations, but the high scores of atypical sulfur graphs do not reveal a missing conventional pharmacophore.

transferable_gaps.evidence: The cited leading aryl-alkyne molecule scores 0.5600222476080907 while carrying a hydrogen-bearing sulfur atom with oxo, carbon and two nitrogen bonds. Related O–F chemistry scores 0.4963704929462404, and a separate carbonyl/piperazine O–F analogue scores 0.21440741901011376. The full output also contains direct N/O/S–halogen bonds. Accepted molecular graphs and favorable scores therefore coexist with chemically questionable connectivity.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator does not consistently preserve ordinary functional-group valence and attachment chemistry when elaborating useful structures.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent functional-group replacements that retain useful surrounding aromatic and polar relationships while distinguishing ordinary amines, amides, oxo-sulfur groups and carbon-bound halogens from unusual heteroatom valence or heteroatom halogenation. Let accepted session feedback compare chemically coherent alternatives; do not treat valence parsing or score alone as evidence of stable chemistry.

transferable_gaps.evidence: One proposal set contains 347 of 870 molecules above 50 heavy atoms, compared with 128 for its Parent, while its leading cited structure has only 23 heavy atoms. Other low tails include methane, OO and OF at 0.0, and large duplicated amine or conjugated-carbonyl structures score 0.03431111746034991 and 2.250908533370224e-18. Some larger molecules still occupy high tails, so a universal small-molecule rule is not supported.
transferable_gaps.gap: Growth and contraction do not reliably preserve an appropriate molecular scale or a coherent useful core.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Provide core-preserving growth, contraction and linker alternatives that can vary size without removing the useful donor, acceptor, amine and aromatic relationships or repeatedly joining whole successful molecules. Determine useful scale from the current accepted observations rather than imposing a task identity or treating size alone as the objective.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Every task digest gives stereocentre_rate 0.0. Read-only RDKit inspection finds unassigned tetrahedral centres in 290, 215, 433, 511 and 298 optimizer rows in the supplied task order and no assigned centres. Cited pyrazoline-like rings, branched aminoalkyl groups and substituted N–N/carbonyl rings provide concrete examples; short closures and ring rearrangements also occur among high-scoring variants.
transferable_gaps.gap: Explicit stereochemistry and controlled ring geometry remain missing even when the output contains configurationally rich structures.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Make specified configurational alternatives and chemically credible ring closure, expansion and contraction available while preserving useful surrounding connectivity. Separate changes in stereochemistry, saturation and ring geometry so their consequences can be learned from accepted feedback. The present absence of specification does not establish a benefit for any chosen configuration.

nodes.method_name: Genetic GFN: reciprocal learning between a flow policy and graph search
nodes.method_thesis: Anchor the root in Genetic GFN: alternately generate molecules with a GFlowNet policy, refine the resulting scored population through graph crossover and mutation, and distill scored descendants back into the policy using rank-weighted off-policy replay. The policy uses trajectory balance with a learned log normalizer and regularization toward a frozen prior. [Kim et al., Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.05961v4) describe this mechanism. Train the prior only on the permitted unlabeled corpus. Each objective starts with clean policy adaptation, replay and population state initialized from its supplied observations. Use a positive terminal reward increasing with the observed maximization score. Schedule policy and genetic phases around the evaluator's announced feedback; both produce new molecules, and all reward-bearing training records come from accepted observations. Later policy samples must enter genetic populations, and accepted graph descendants must affect subsequent policy updates. Generate further valid, canonical-unique structures to fill announced batches, without corpus ranking or a fixed molecular library. The hypothesis is that learned global proposals propagate local discoveries into new promising regions and then support further graph refinement, raising the mean of five independent final Top-1 scores. Published larger-budget gains do not establish that this reciprocal learning becomes useful quickly enough here.

approach.method_basis: The Parent evolves a live population of scored molecular graphs. It keeps the highest-scoring survivors, favors their upper score bands when choosing parents, and makes new graphs through mutation chains and connected-fragment crossover. Every accepted score also enters a complete archive used by a count-fingerprint Gaussian process to choose each evaluation batch from a larger candidate pool. Direct aromatic carbon/nitrogen exchange is disabled. Accepted offspring can become parents, while the best observed molecule remains in the population.
approach.novelty: This control tests the contribution of greedy survival among records other than the incumbent. It always keeps the inherited best record, fills the remaining survivor places with the most recently accepted records still in the live contest, and restores the original score order before breeding. Unlike the initial-cohort and uniform-parent controls, it keeps recursive breeding and the original rank preference. Unlike the recent-batch tie experiment, it deliberately removes competition by strict score among nonincumbents. Retention receipts will be followed through actual breeding support, draws and evaluated descendants; recency is an explicit contribution control, not a proposed performance gain.

nodes.hypothesis: Replace only nonincumbent score-greedy survivor membership with the newest accepted serials from the current live retention contest, protecting the single inherited incumbent and restoring inherited score/serial order before unchanged breeding.

finding_summary.headline: Nonincumbent greedy survival contributes: recency changes breeding and lowers mean final score by 0.011807.
finding_summary.insights:
The result supplies positive conditional evidence for inherited nonincumbent greedy survival while the incumbent, score-quantile sampling, recursive feedback and learned allocation stay active. Its observed route is changed access to shared survivors, rather than reuse of the extra weak records kept at the local cutoff. The latter route is explicitly refuted here. Most changed memberships leave the immediate sampling probabilities unchanged; preserving a molecule is therefore not the same as exploring its neighborhood. Earlier protected-but-never-bred retention failures remain relevant counterexamples.

The shared-survivor route can still produce useful chemistry: a crossover involving a parent newly inside sampling support creates a halogen-free aromatic/carbonyl leader and then breeds 243 times. Another such crossover loses to its parents and never breeds again. The molecular assessment finds many tiny recency-only records and 16 tiny final survivors, alongside useful amines and carbonyl frameworks and persistent reactive bonds, unusual rings and unspecified stereochemistry. These observations explain what was retained and used; they do not establish a chemical cause of the aggregate loss, graph-equivalence guarantees, or practical chemical feasibility.

This answers the specified retention-component contrast on the complete three-seed panel. It leaves membership quality, age, rank changes and later learning bundled together, and does not measure the whole evolutionary foundation or combine additively with the separate rank-preference and recursive-breeding controls. The six endpoint gains and the zero-use pathways limit transfer beyond the registered conditions. No age-window or retention retuning is justified by this completed control.
finding_summary.results:
The rule executed exactly in all 4,365 retention calls. It changed 3,483 of 3,540 capacity-limited survivor sets and 3,451 retained score vectors while preserving the incumbent. Stored alternatives did not become new breeders: none of the 135 recency-only records ever gained later sampling support or bred. Shared survivors did change ranks and probabilities, producing 3,865 altered-rank parent draws and 713 altered-probability draws. Their accepted products numbered 126 and 18 respectively, with the latter inside the former; three of the 126 raised the incumbent and 58 later bred. Two task/seed sessions had affected draws but no immediately accepted product in this locally tagged cohort.

All three replicas completed. Mean final Top -1 fell from 0.595670 to 0.583863, a paired change of -0.011807 beyond the registered 0.002 scale. Seed changes were -0.044786, +0.024951 and -0.015585. Nine task/seed endpoints declined and six improved; decoration hopping, docking and median-task means declined, while zaleplon and sitagliptin means improved. Seed-macro population deviation fell from 0.026593 to 0.002305. All 4,350 accepted products survived their immediate batch and 2,746 later bred, versus 3,415 and 2,401 under the Parent, yet this greater survival and reuse did not produce a higher endpoint mean.

molecular.headline: Aromatic carbonyl and amine families persist; recency-only survivors stay outside breeding support.
molecular.overall_character:
The complete Child and matched Parent panels cover all five objectives and Search seeds 0, 1 and 2: 4,500 scored records per node, including 4,350 accepted optimizer products and 150 initial records. All 30 trusted trajectories and 30 corresponding candidate logs were read. Each task has 870 optimizer products across its three seeds. All fifteen Child/Parent trajectories differ, with no score disagreement for a shared molecular identity within a matched task/seed. There are no missing paths or unmatched seeds. Source, trajectory, log and historical-evidence hashes, molecule descriptors, chronological provenance and trusted citations are retained in .slots/r0020-02-ablation-L01/molecular/; trajectory_chemistry_audit.json, retention_exposure_audit.json, selected_chemistry_audit.json and validation.json are the detailed receipts.

These are mostly aromatic, heteroatom-rich ring assemblies with amides, ketones, cyclic carbonyls, imines, ethers and amines, often heavily modified by halogens. Median heavy-atom counts in the fixed task order are 25, 31, 31, 31 and 27, versus Parent 25, 33, 31, 30 and 27. Overall the Child median is 29 heavy atoms and four perceived rings; individual evaluated structures range from one to 107 heavy atoms. Within each seed, related aromatic/carbonyl or aryl-amine families recur despite many distinct strings. Across all optimizer rows, Child / Parent molecule counts are 897 / 1,042 with N–halogen bonds, 456 / 278 with O–halogen bonds, 319 / 273 with O–O bonds, 24 / 17 with ring triple bonds, and 25 / 42 with a ring carbon carrying two double bonds. These flags overlap and are structural cautions, not measured stability, synthesis, toxicity or safety outcomes. Useful halogen-free leaders and conventional amine/carbonyl arrangements are counterexamples to a universal requirement for reactive bonds. RDKit identifies unassigned stereocentres in 2,553 / 2,408 molecules; no stereochemical assignments appear in the Child digest counters.

Retention and real chemical use differ sharply. Of 135 distinct records retained against a same-contest greedy cap, 125 are generated accepted products and ten are initial records. Their median size is three heavy atoms, with 79 at most three heavy atoms; larger examples include modified heterocyclic carbonyls and duplicated multiring frameworks. Although 124 subsequently occur in a live breeding population, none reaches positive breeding support or is drawn after its first recency-only retention. Eleven never appear in a later live state, including two first protected during terminal feedback. This is a measured lack of downstream use of that particular set, not absence of other chemically useful recency-retained records. The comparison is always the current Child live population plus the newly accepted record, never a resurrected archive or a separately executed greedy future.

The other observed route involves shared survivors whose ranks change. Their actual draws enter 3,051 pool products and 126 evaluated products: 12 exceed the best generating-parent score, four tie and 110 fall below it; three update the sequential incumbent, 58 later breed and 51 remain in final populations. The subset with changed sampling probability enters 548 pool products and 18 evaluations, with three parent beats and one incumbent update; these cohorts overlap. One session leader comes from a shared parent promoted across the support boundary, described below. Unqueried pool products have no assigned outcomes. Across all products, every Child product survives its immediate batch, versus 3,415 for the Parent; 2,746 / 2,401 distinct products later breed and 960 / 960 remain at termination. The Child final survivors include 16 tiny fragments versus none for the Parent, as well as 238 N–halogen-, 134 O–halogen- and 63 O–O-bearing records versus 287, 55 and 38. Final membership is not validation of chemistry. The last 150 evaluated products per node have no later breeding opportunity; the terminal leaders in two sessions cannot support a descendant claim.

The supplied complete paired mean is 0.583862951276973 versus 0.5956696497334577, with seed changes -0.04478568415133899, +0.02495097723246098 and -0.015585388450575999. Six task/seed endpoints improve and nine decline. These outcomes accompany changed chemistry; they do not identify a molecular mediator. The scoped control leaves incumbent protection, score-quantile sampling and partner exclusion, recursive accepted-offspring breeding, the complete accepted archive and active count-GP allocation in place. Historical recent-tie retention n-03acfe1ba8af also had 145 newly protected records that never subsequently bred, despite other rank-based exposure; older core-round retention n-28dc36ed5be7 had 602 directly protected records outside later support under a different Parent and profile. Their losses and limitations remain counterexamples. Uniform-live breeding n-a56491c332aa and initial-cohort breeding n-4d4b5eafa8b3 address different conditional boundaries on the shared current Parent, not independent or additive whole-foundation effects. The supplied catalog still has incomplete historical review and partial L07 ordinary-continuation composition. This assessment neither closes those gaps nor decides activation, contribution or eligibility.

per_task.generated_character:
The 870 products are mainly medium-sized indole-like, ring-expanded nitrogen heterocycle and aryl-carbonyl structures: median 25 heavy atoms and three perceived rings, with 375 N–halogen-bearing molecules. Seed 0 evaluation 207 reaches 0.459794 with a 24-heavy-atom, four-ring methoxy/methyl-substituted assembly bearing an N-amino aryl amide and a thiol substituent. It is halogen-free. Seed 1 evaluation 269 reaches 0.440491 with a 25-heavy-atom aromatic nitrogen ring expanded to nine atoms, an N–Br bond and a pyridyl ester. Seed 2 evaluation 187 reaches 0.433013 with a 24-heavy-atom indole/pyridyl ketone carrying N-vinyl and O-vinyl substituents, without halogens. These are distinct chemical organizations, not uniform enrichment of one halogenated motif.

The Parent leaders instead include a cumulated-carbon anilino/pyridyl arrangement in seed 0, an N-fluorinated heteroaryl amide in seed 1, and an N-chlorinated aryl dicarbonyl in seed 2. Complete matched final-best Child / Parent scores are seed 0: 0.459794 / 0.394051 (+0.065743); seed 1: 0.440491 / 0.474117 (-0.033626); seed 2: 0.433013 / 0.438973 (-0.005960).

The seed 2 leader is a recorded pure-crossover product. One shared survivor, the brominated indole/unsaturated seven-membered oxygen-ring ketone at evaluation 154 (0.339176), occupies actual partner rank 31 versus rank 32 under the last same-contest greedy list; the other parent scores 0.423990. The product exceeds that better parent by 0.009022 and later serves in 243 breeding draws, yet its final session endpoint remains below the matched Parent. This links real chemistry to a used shared survivor, not a directly recency-only molecule or proof that a particular inherited group caused success. Across this task, 51 evaluated products have a shared changed-rank parent: five parent beats, three ties and 43 losses. The 25 directly recency-only records never breed after protection.
liabilities: Frequent N–halogen substitution, an N-amino amide, a charged N–N environment and a nine-member aromatic nitrogen ring warrant compound-specific feasibility assessment. Parsing and high scores are insufficient evidence of makeability.

Twenty-five products have at most three heavy atoms, and recency can retain such fragments without giving them later reproductive access; membership is not evidence that useful chemical coverage increased.
missing_features: The evaluated panel does not show a consistently ordinary-bond, chemically coherent series preserving its better aromatic/carbonyl arrangements across ring-size changes; the halogen-free leaders show that a blanket halogen requirement would be wrong.

Controlled stereochemical and geometric alternatives are not demonstrated. Scalar scores do not reveal which unobserved target motif, if any, is missing; absence from the evaluated stream cannot establish absence from unscored proposals.
per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The observed gradient favors a substantial aromatic carbonyl framework over stripped fragments. Initial seed 0 evaluation 9, a trimethoxy indole carboxamide, scores 0.305105; the highest 50 products have median 25 heavy atoms, while the lowest 50 have median 3.5. Vinyl fluoride at seed 0 evaluation 257 scores zero. Size alone does not account for the gradient: ring rearrangements, carbonyl placement and substitution change the scores within similarly sized families.

Higher scores coexist with questionable bonds. Seed 0 evaluation 222 reaches 0.449897 with both N–Cl and N–F, while the halogen-free seed 0 leader scores higher. The charged N–N carbonyl substituent at evaluation 213 reaches 0.425403, beats its generating parent and later breeds 105 times. Thus neither N–halogen presence nor absence is a general score explanation. The final seed 0 product at evaluation 300 falls to 0.377678 while carrying an N–S–Cl branch and N–F; retained incumbent score should not be confused with that last product.

liabilities: There are 181 O–halogen-, 240 O–O- and 24 ring-triple-bond-bearing products, versus Parent 89, 218 and 17. These overlapping groups include peroxide/hypohalite environments and constrained ring unsaturation that require local chemical assessment.

Crowded fused systems, unusual carbon substitution and occasional very large assemblies coexist with the aromatic frameworks. Recency-only preservation gives no synthesis or stability evidence, and the directly protected examples supply no descendant outcomes.
missing_features: A consistently feasible set of alternative linker and ring connections preserving the higher-scoring heteroaryl/carbonyl organization is not established. Scalar ties tolerate materially different reactive substitutions.

The evaluated higher-ring-count products do not demonstrate reliable improvement through controlled scaffold reorganization; unscored pool structures cannot be assigned the same limitation without labels.
per_task.score_gradient_reading:
The initial seed 0 aromatic cyclic-dione/ester at evaluation 7 scores 0.548381. Larger, connected heteroaryl carbonyl organizations rise above the 0.5 fragment floor; the highest 50 Child products have median 30 heavy atoms and four aromatic rings, versus 7.5 heavy atoms in the lowest 50. The observed association does not imply that maximizing ring number is useful: the seven-ring seed 0 leader remains far below its matched Parent.

Different chemistry can share the same top score: seed 1 evaluation 224 has methoxy and O–Br substituents, while evaluation 234 replaces the methoxy organization with another O–Br-containing arrangement and still scores 0.643167. Forty-six of the highest 50 products carry O–halogen bonds. This is evidence of tolerance in the recorded score, not a demonstrated need for those bonds or a chemically validated analogue series.

per_task.generated_character:

nodes.method_name: Mol GA: rank-selected de novo graph evolution
nodes.method_thesis: Anchor the root in Mol GA: maintain a population of oracle-evaluated molecular graphs, sample breeding parents across high-ranked quantiles, generate new offspring through graph crossover and atom/bond mutations, and update survivors greedily after each observation. These are the proposal and selection mechanisms described by [Tripp and Hernández-Lobato (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.09267v1). Start from the supplied initial observations and incorporate newly evaluated offspring immediately, following the evaluator's announced batching. Repeated graph edits and recombination create an evolving search space; no corpus ranking, stored molecule library, pretrained model, or fixed candidate enumeration is needed. The causal hypothesis is that direct selection on task-local scores concentrates successive structural changes around improving molecules quickly enough to raise the final best observed score. The published evidence concerns a larger-budget AUC-Top-10 setting, so its transfer to this benchmark's final Top-1 objective remains a hypothesis.

approach.method_basis: The Parent evolves molecular graphs from a bounded population of accepted high-scoring molecules. Score-quantile parent sampling, connected-fragment crossover and local graph mutations create a fresh surplus pool. It retains stable canonical identity admission and a formula-preserving aromatic nitrogen-position exchange. A Gaussian process trained on every earlier accepted score predicts the pool using binary local-environment fingerprints, and correlated posterior draws choose evaluations. Feedback updates both the breeding population and the full prediction archive. Its posterior always uses the same small standardized noise scale, regardless of disagreement between molecular similarity and the accepted scores.
approach.novelty: Learn that one noise scale from the current accepted archive. At each fit, compare a fixed small ladder of noise scales by Gaussian marginal likelihood and condition the existing posterior with the best-supported value. This lets observed score relationships determine how strongly the model interpolates nearby molecules and how much uncertainty remains. The earlier posterior sibling changed binary environment presence to counts while retaining fixed noise; this experiment keeps the Parent representation and tests feedback-dependent regularization as a separate mechanism. Earlier graph and parent-allocation mechanisms remain inherited.

nodes.hypothesis: Select the Gaussian process observation-noise scale at each fit by accepted-archive marginal likelihood over a fixed ladder around the inherited scale, so task-local label agreement controls posterior regularization.

finding_summary.headline: Learned noise improved selected-stream error and coverage, but mean search score fell 0.015961
finding_summary.insights: The experiment separates a real regularization benefit from a search benefit. The strongest controlled prediction improvement occurs in sitagliptin: latent coverage rises from 466 to 558 of 870 scored molecules, with lower MSE in all three seeds. DRD2 instead loses three covered molecules on the same scored identities, and ranking deteriorates in the pooled comparison. Thus reducing average prediction error and winning training likelihood do not establish better discrimination among the next candidates to evaluate. The frequent upper and lower boundary choices show that different accepted molecular/score relationships call for very different regularization; they leave the adequacy of the finite ladder unresolved. Substantial undercoverage remains even with learned noise, particularly in the harder streams. Scalar noise cannot distinguish molecules with identical binary fingerprints or correct every mismatch in the representation and mean model. The chemical assessment also finds recurring ring-rich families with more reactive N/O-halogen and peroxide motifs, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry, so these predictive gains supply no evidence that chemical liabilities were repaired. The measured same-data comparison supports a modest, heterogeneous prediction benefit. It cannot assign counterfactual scores to unselected molecules or identify which changed choices caused the loss in whole-search endpoints. The mechanism executed; the expected score improvement did not occur.
finding_summary.results: Noise selection changed the implemented posterior in 434 of 435 fits, and every likelihood winner and recorded evaluation choice reconstructed correctly. The smallest available noise won 179 fits and the largest won 116; the chosen scale changed after feedback at 41 of 420 opportunities. On the same earlier archives and the same 4350 subsequently scored molecules, prediction MSE fell from 0.0121771 with fixed noise to 0.0116233 with learned noise. Latent 95% interval coverage rose from 79.75% to 82.51%, while mean within-batch rank correlation fell from 0.41596 to 0.39609. Noise-inclusive coverage reached 89.91% with wider intervals, reported separately from latent uncertainty. The same random draws applied to the two distributions changed the selected molecule set in 255 of 435 batches. Despite those prediction gains, mean final-best score fell from 0.551771 to 0.535810, a paired change of -0.015961 against the registered +0.002 target; seed variability increased from 0.008223 to 0.023346. One seed macro improved and two declined. Task means rose for median and sitagliptin and slightly for decoration, but fell for DRD2 and zaleplon. All tasks completed their budgets, and every factorization succeeded at the first jitter.

molecular.headline: Ring-rich molecules retain reactive substituents, oversized assemblies and unresolved stereochemistry
molecular.overall_character: This assessment covers every supplied trajectory for node n-9002c3d22369 and parent n-9edaa26007c3: all five objectives and seeds 0, 1 and 2, with 900 observations and 870 optimizer proposals per objective in each node. The digest's tasks_without_trajectories list is empty. Its initial excerpt represents seed 0 and its final excerpt represents seed 2; the full trajectories were read to cover the other seeds. The molecules contain abundant phenyl and aza-aromatic rings, fused and bridged heterocycles, carbonyl groups, ethers, amines and halogens. Different seeds retain different families, including indole carboxamides, thiocarbonyl-linked pyrazoles, repeated carbonyl-bearing heteroaryls, aryl-linked cyclic amines and annulated dicarbonyl heterocycles. Structural diversity is moderate across the panel but uneven within the stronger examples. SMILES uniqueness alone would overstate chemically useful diversity. The digest's ring-closure rates range from 0.9609 to 0.9908 and aromatic-token presence rates from 0.9460 to 0.9908; these are fractions of proposal strings, not atom fractions or perceived ring counts. Passive RDKit 2023.09.6 parsing succeeds for all 4350 generated records per node. The child has a median of 31 heavy atoms, 5 perceived rings and 3 aromatic rings; the parent has 30, 5 and 3. Child N-halogen-bearing, O-halogen-bearing and O-O-bearing molecule counts are 870, 375 and 161, compared with 667, 319 and 85 in the parent. These structural alerts require chemical context: a valid graph is not a synthesis or stability demonstration, and an N-S bond by itself is not an objection. Some conventional aromatic amides and amine scaffolds look tractable, but the repeated reactive groups and large or unusually connected ring systems make overall synthetic plausibility questionable and drug-likeness weak. Every generated SMILES is formally uncharged and lacks specified tetrahedral or double-bond stereochemistry; RDKit identifies unassigned tetrahedral centres in 2200 child molecules. Basic amines nevertheless occur prominently, so the charge encoding does not establish solution-state neutrality. All score statements below reuse observed labels; no new molecular scoring, activation judgement, synthesis calculation or target-specific pharmacophore inference was performed. Numeric graph descriptions, full file hashes and seed comparisons are reproducible from /projects/standard/adeshwal/shared/zhou2577/SPIRAL/runs/SPIRAL2/policy/responses/r0011-08-improve-L01-molecular-audit.json and its adjacent passive audit script.

per_task.generated_character: These are mainly compact ring-rich heteroaromatics: the proposal median is 25 heavy atoms. Seed 0's stronger family contains phenolic pyrazoles with thiocarbonyl linkers and small unsaturated carbocycles, including a cyclobutenol and a cyclopentadiene in its best molecule. Seeds 1 and 2 favour alkoxy/alkyl-substituted indoles bearing pyridyl carboxamides. Each seed's best molecule has 25 heavy atoms; seed 0 has 4 perceived rings, while seeds 1 and 2 have 3. The seed-1 best retains a conventional secondary amide with carbon-bound halogens; the seed-2 best instead has an N-F amide. The latter remains a recognisable medicinal scaffold but has a chemically consequential substituent on its amide nitrogen. Later seed-2 molecules also contain rearranged annulated N/O ring systems, thiocarbonyls and O-F bonds. The digest records ring-closure presence 0.9770, aromatic-token presence 0.9598 and halogen presence 0.7598.
liabilities: N-F amides occur among the highest-scoring molecules, and 258 of 870 proposals have an N-halogen bond. The conventional secondary amide in the cited seed-1 best shows that useful observed scores can coexist with a more ordinary linkage.

The cyclobutenol/thiocarbonyl family and later heavily annulated structures raise stability, strain and synthetic-route questions. O-F-bearing late products and tiny oxidising or halogen fragments further show that sanitisation does not enforce ordinary medicinal chemistry.
missing_features: The supported opportunity is a wider set of compact heteroatom and carbonyl arrangements with intact ordinary amide connectivity. transferable_gaps.evidence: Among 4350 generated child molecules, 870 contain N-halogen bonds, 375 contain O-halogen bonds and 161 contain O-O bonds; the corresponding parent counts are 667, 319 and 85. transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support chemically contextual substitutions and intact-group alternatives around amides, ethers, amines and sulfur centres. Generate alternatives from existing graphs and let accepted feedback establish their value; distinguish reactive N/O-halogen or peroxy connections from ordinary carbon-bound halogens, rather than treating all halogens or all N-S bonds alike.

transferable_gaps.evidence: One supplied stream has a median of 69 heavy atoms and reaches 120, with an 84-heavy-atom digest-best molecule, whereas other digest examples collapse to methane, acetylene or tiny halogen fragments with very low labels. Stronger compact molecules also exist. Molecular growth, chemical complexity and observed score therefore have different relationships across the supplied streams.
transferable_gaps.gap: The output lacks reliable control over both excessive fragment accumulation and destructive collapse of useful molecular cores.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Provide bounded core-preserving growth, contraction and connected-fragment replacement, with explicit attention to retained functional groups and molecular size. Learn which variants help from the current accepted molecular/score history, without fixing a universal preferred size or forcing either growth or pruning.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Every digest task has stereocentre_rate 0.0. Passive RDKit reading identifies unassigned tetrahedral centres in 2200 of 4350 generated child molecules, while finding no assigned tetrahedral centres or specified double-bond stereo. Cited examples include substituted cyclic amines, cyclobutenol, acetal-like carbons and substituted alkenes.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator produces stereogenic structures without demonstrated stereochemical resolution or coverage.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent and preserve existing stereochemical information through graph changes and provide bounded chemically feasible stereoisomer alternatives where new centres or alkene geometry arise. Their value remains a hypothesis to test using ordinary accepted feedback; an unspecified SMILES does not demonstrate exploration of all its stereoisomers.

transferable_gaps.evidence: All digest charged_rate values are 0.0, and all 4350 child proposal graphs have zero formal charge. Some of the strongest cited structures nevertheless contain cyclic amines, secondary amines and amidines; other abundant nitrogens are amide-like or aromatic. Neutral encoding therefore conceals chemically different ionisation possibilities.
transferable_gaps.gap: The output contains potentially ionisable motifs but demonstrates no explicit charge-state alternatives.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Distinguish nitrogen environments and support chemically valid state alternatives using only molecular structure, ordinary identity admission and accepted labels. Preserve clarity about the proposed chemical state; no particular charge, pKa or environmental protonation state follows from these observed scores alone.

transferable_gaps.evidence: The panel includes rich rings and multiple families, yet stronger digest examples repeatedly occupy substituted indole carboxamides, repeated carbonyl-bearing heteroaryls, aryl-linked N-rings and annulated dicarbonyl scaffolds. Several large, visibly different structures receive the same recorded label, and some seed families retain the parent's best identity. These observations do not support equating string novelty with new useful chemistry.
transferable_gaps.gap: Useful structural coverage remains uneven despite abundant rings and many distinct molecular strings.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Expand scaffold and ring-connection alternatives that preserve useful donor/acceptor arrangements at comparable size, alongside local substitutions. Assess coverage by molecular cores and intact functional groups, using accepted feedback to discover where a new topology matters; do not prescribe a benchmark-specific scaffold or assume that adding rings improves coverage.

nodes.method_name: Mol GA: rank-selected de novo graph evolution
nodes.method_thesis: Anchor the root in Mol GA: maintain a population of oracle-evaluated molecular graphs, sample breeding parents across high-ranked quantiles, generate new offspring through graph crossover and atom/bond mutations, and update survivors greedily after each observation. These are the proposal and selection mechanisms described by [Tripp and Hernández-Lobato (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.09267v1). Start from the supplied initial observations and incorporate newly evaluated offspring immediately, following the evaluator's announced batching. Repeated graph edits and recombination create an evolving search space; no corpus ranking, stored molecule library, pretrained model, or fixed candidate enumeration is needed. The causal hypothesis is that direct selection on task-local scores concentrates successive structural changes around improving molecules quickly enough to raise the final best observed score. The published evidence concerns a larger-budget AUC-Top-10 setting, so its transfer to this benchmark's final Top-1 objective remains a hypothesis.

retained_mechanisms: Task-local scored molecular-graph population with score-ranked parent sampling across three high-ranked quantiles.
De novo connected-fragment graph crossover.
Local atom/bond mutations with inherited inner retries and occasional multistep graph walks.

Direct formula-preserving C/N positional exchange within an eligible aromatic six-member ring, appended to the inherited uniformly sampled per-site replacement menu with ordinary aromaticity, checking and novelty gates.
Chemical sanitization and pool-only stable canonical identity admission, preserving the checked graph under admitted normalization and boundedly rejecting unresolved representations.
Bounded greedy score-ranked survival and breeding from accepted offspring, with a separate complete ordered accepted-score archive.
Task-local binary Morgan/Tanimoto Gaussian-process conditioning with unit amplitude, empirical score normalization, cached features and bounded Cholesky retries.
Correlated latent posterior draws over fresh surplus pools, sequential masked maximizers, feedback refitting, previous-emission probes and inherited explicit numerical fallback.
Accepted-archive marginal-likelihood observation-noise selection over the fixed seven-point ladder, with deterministic exact-tie ordering and reuse of the winning training factor and coefficients.

approach.method_basis: The Parent trains a recurrent SMILES language model on an unlabeled molecular corpus, then starts each objective with an independent policy copied from that frozen prior. After accepted feedback, it trains on the best-scoring half of the current batch and the highest-scoring eligible historical elites. A bounded memory preserves the original accepted strings and scores of its thirty-two strongest elites. Each selected sequence has equal loss weight and a target equal to its frozen-prior log probability plus sixty times its accepted score. The policy takes a bounded series of clipped Adam steps toward those targets, then directly samples complete SMILES; chemical validation and canonical duplicate rejection fill the announced batch. Its stronger-history selector is already active, but the optimizer can still move away from the historical examples it selected.
approach.novelty: Add a projection of the actual proposed Adam step onto the historical loss's locally non-increasing directions. At each step, measure the historical loss gradient before Adam moves. If Adam's proposed parameter displacement points toward increasing that loss, remove just that component and retain the rest of the displacement. This tests whether preserving local historical fitting can help strong accepted examples influence later novel molecules. The earlier checkpoint experiment selected a lower-loss state from an update path and sometimes discarded all early progress; this change keeps Adam's moments and counters and leaves current-only initialization intact. The target-normalization sibling changed what every selected string should fit and suffered completion failures; this change retains the Parent's targets. Prior-training and replay-membership siblings did not constrain the realized optimizer displacement. The projection protects a first-order direction, so finite fitting gains and useful generation still need measurement.

nodes.hypothesis: Project each proposed online Adam parameter displacement onto the half-space that does not increase the fixed selected-historical augmented-target loss to first order, using that loss's gradient at the pre-step policy, while retaining the inherited equal-row objective, Adam moments and step counter.

finding_summary.headline: Historical slope protection worked, but finite fitting gains did not improve molecular scores.
finding_summary.insights:
The experiment establishes that adverse directions in the actual Adam displacement can be removed while preserving the optimizer's accumulated state and the original learning problem. Exact initialization controls, unchanged targets and verified state preservation rule out those confounds. The practical limit is visible within the same step: a first-order constraint usually softens historical error growth, but curvature often leaves a finite increase. Protecting the historical group also leaves individual historical rows unprotected and can sacrifice progress on the current batch.

The targets continue to ask for impossible positive log probabilities in 607 of 2,100 nonterminal historical exposures, compared with 595 in the Parent. Better protection of such fitting pressure has no demonstrated link to more useful molecules. Total chemical diversity also fails to explain the score loss: after historical updates, sitagliptin proposals covered 767 distinct molecular cores versus 714 in the Parent, yet only 142 proposals exceeded the common initial best score, versus 189. The molecular assessment describes abundant rings and aromatic fragments with uneven placement of useful polar groups and linkers. The open problem is consistently producing productive arrangements within that broad chemistry. These observations narrow the question to the connection between selected-history fitting, finite update tradeoffs and useful future proposals; the projection's execution is established.
finding_summary.results:
The projection executed on 2,029 of 5,040 history-bearing Adam steps followed by further proposals. All 1,904 corrections above the registered numerical resolution measurably changed the parameters and satisfied the intended historical-loss half-space. The remaining 125 triggering corrections were below analytical resolution. Projection affected 381 of the 420 nonterminal historical updates; 99 additional terminal projections have no later molecules to influence. Original accepted strings, scores, targets, replay selection, equal row weights, Adam moments and counters, and frozen priors were preserved. All fifteen current-only initialization updates and first generated batches matched the Parent exactly.

On the same training tensor, the applied projection reduced historical MSE relative to the proposed Adam state in 2,019 of 2,029 nonterminal projected steps, by 1.320902 on average. Current MSE increased relative to that proposal by 0.885112 on average, with worse current fitting in 1,379 steps. Despite satisfying the local slope constraint, 1,807 projected steps still increased historical MSE relative to their own starting state. Across complete updates, historical group error worsened 118 times out of 420, compared with 131 for the Parent. Individual historical rows showed almost no improvement in worsening frequency: 837 of 2,100 exposures worsened, versus 834.

All fifteen tasks completed their 300-call budgets. In subsequent generation, raw validity was 92.56% versus the Parent's 92.67%, novel yield rose from 50.59% to 51.59%, and duplicate draws fell from 42.08% to 40.98%. Sampling nevertheless had a worse tail: 49 batches needed additional sampling, versus 41.

Mean final Top-1 fell from 0.513272 to 0.493473, a paired mean change of -0.019800. All three seed changes were negative: -0.006076, -0.012316 and -0.041007. The child population standard deviation was 0.013845, versus 0.001984 for the Parent. Sitagliptin accounted for the main loss, falling from mean 0.288538 to 0.172377. Zaleplon improved by 0.023783 and DRD2 by 0.001335, while deco-hop and median-2 decreased by 0.005779 and 0.002176. The expected score improvement was not observed.
